title: Probabilistic SLO Headroom and Tenancy Reconciliation Playbook
author: Asha Patel
body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook codifies a probabilistic, tenant-aware approach to SLO headroom calculation and reconciliation. It is intended for SREs and platform engineers responsible for multi-tenant inference capacity planning, incident response where SLO degradation is capacity-driven, and post-incident forensic analysis.

Scope: Applies to Redwood hosted and Dedicated inference services (model-serving clusters) where tenants are logically isolated but share heterogeneous GPU pools. Does not replace contractual capacity commitments for Dedicated customers; it augments them with probabilistic signals that improve runtime resilience for shared clusters.

Why this exists

Traditional static headroom targets (e.g., keep 20% spare capacity) do not capture burstiness in inference workloads or correlated tenant spikes. We instead model headroom probabilistically from tenant-level usage distributions and SLO expenditure traces, and provide concrete reconciliation steps when SLOs degrade. This reduces unnecessary overprovisioning while preserving customer-facing reliability.

Key concepts and definitions

- Headroom: the capacity margin expressed as a probability that the cluster can absorb an additional X RPS for Y minutes without breaching p99 latency SLO.
- Burn profile: time-series of SLO error budget consumption per tenant and per model route.
- Tenancy risk score: composite score for each tenant computed from burst factor, historical variance, contractual tier, and active change events.
- Admission controller: runtime gate that admits or rejects requests when capacity budget threatens SLOs.
- Soft eviction: non-destructive mitigation that reduces tenant concurrency or reroutes to lower-cost model variants.
- Hard eviction: temporary suspension of non-critical tenant traffic (last resort).

Ownership and contacts

- Playbook owner: Eng-SRE Capacity & Forecasting team (primary contact: Asha Patel, asha.patel@redwood.ai).
- Escalation: On-call SRE -> Capacity lead -> Platform infra manager. See oncall roster for pager details.

Prerequisites and telemetry

Before executing any reconciliation steps, ensure the following telemetry is available and validated:

- Per-tenant RPS and token-counts, 1s granularity for the last 60 minutes.
- Latency quantiles (p50/p95/p99) per route and per GPU pool, 10s rollups for last 24h.
- Error budget burn rate per tenant (1m and 1h windows).
- Model load selectors: mapping of model variants to kernel footprints (GPU memory/compute).
- Admission controller logs and past decisions (allow/deny counts).

Required dashboards and queries

Create/confirm these dashboards exist:

- Headroom Probability Dashboard (cluster-level): shows probability curve of sustaining +10%, +25% RPS for next 30/60/120 minutes.
- Tenant Risk Matrix: tenants on X axis (by risk score), Y axis current burn rate vs. committed rate.
- Eviction Impact Simulator: synthetic scenario selector that computes estimated SLO delta when reducing concurrency for top N tenants.

Operational policy: trigger conditions

Trigger to enter reconciliation mode (one or more conditions):

1) Cluster p99 latency exceeds SLO by >10% for >5 minutes.
2) Cluster headroom probability for sustaining +10% RPS in next 30m drops below 75%.
3) Aggregate 1h error budget consumption across the cluster exceeds 50% of total for any single tenant group.

Decision matrix (quick guide)

- If p99 > SLO and headroom prob < 50%: escalate to emergency capacity runbook (hard eviction window candidate).
- If p99 > SLO but headroom prob 50-75%: enter mitigations lane (soft eviction + admission rebalancing) and schedule 1h re-eval.
- If p99 within SLO but burn-rate rising steeply: preemptive throttling for top 5 highest-risk tenants.

Reconciliation runbook (step-by-step)

1) Triage and evidence collection (SRE oncall)
   a) Pull Headroom Probability Dashboard and snapshot the probability curve for +10% and +25% RPS.
   b) Query per-tenant 1m/5m RPS and token counts for the last 30 minutes. CLI example: 
      curl -s "https://telemetry.redwood/api/query" -d '{"q":"tenant.rps{pool=\"gpu-cluster-eu\"}[30m]"}' | jq '.'
   c) Export recent admission controller logs: allow/deny counts and reasons for last 10 minutes.
   d) Record any recent deployments or config changes (CI/CD tags) in the incident timeline.

2) Classify dominant cause (SRE)
   - Resource saturation: high GPU util + memory pressure; kernel queue growth.
   - Tenant burst: small set of tenants producing disproportionate traffic.
   - Anomalous model: new model variant has longer inference tail.
   - Routing/fallback thrash: repeated fallback to heavier model variants.

3) Apply mitigations in containment window (15–30 minutes)
   Order matters: prefer non-customer-visible actions first.

   a) Reduce concurrency for non-critical tenants by 20% using the admission controller. Command example: 
      platformctl admission set-limit --tenant-id tenant-123 --concurrency 80%

   b) Trigger KV prefix cache retention boost on hot models (if applicable). This reduces cold-start token overhead.

   c) Reroute heavy tail traffic to quantized/cheaper model variant if quality SLO tolerances allow. Use rollout policy with automatic rollback on quality regression.

   d) If instability continues, enable short-lived per-tenant rate limits that preserve critical SLAs: 
      platformctl quota update --tenant tenant-456 --window 60s --max-requests 3000

4) Escalation to emergency capacity (if mitigations fail)
   Criteria: after 30 mins mitigations are insufficient and p99 remains > SLO.

   a) Engage Capacity lead to evaluate fast provisioning options (elastic reservoir, cross-region shift).
   b) If immediate capacity is not feasible, coordinate hard eviction as a last resort: remove or pause lowest-tier non-enterprise tenants until SLOs restore. Document tenant IDs and duration.

5) Post-incident reconciliation (within 24–72 hours)
   a) Run probabilistic re-simulation using retained telemetry: sample tenant burst distributions and compute required provisioning to achieve 95% headroom probability for +25% RPS.
   b) Produce a remediation ticket with estimated cost delta and suggested long-term mitigations (e.g., reserve burst capacity, improve model quantization, split hot tenants into dedicated pools).
   c) Schedule a blameless postmortem and include the probabilistic analysis artifacts.

Forensics checklist for incident review

- Attach headroom probability snapshots for 5, 15, 30, 60, 120-minute horizons.
- List top 10 tenants by contribution to burn during incident window (by token count and error budget).
- Evidence of admission controller activity and timestamps.
- Kernel queue length and GPU memory pressure traces.
- CI/CD deployment markers and config changes correlated to incident start.

Parameter table: thresholds and actions

Metric | Threshold | Window | Immediate Action
-------|-----------|--------|----------------
cluster.p99_latency / SLO | > 110% | 5m | Enter mitigation lane, notify oncall
headroom.prob(+10% RPS) | < 75% | 10m | Apply soft eviction + prioritize critical tenants
headroom.prob(+25% RPS) | < 50% | 10m | Consider emergency capacity, prepare hard eviction list
tenant.burn_rate | > 50% of cluster | 1h | Throttle or quota top contributors, create remediation ticket
inflight.kernel_queue | > 90% of safe | 1m | Immediate admission reduction for affected pool

(Note: the table above is intended as a quick-reference. Exact numeric thresholds must be approved by SLO governance during large changes.)

Tooling and automation recipes

- Headroom simulator: repository (infra/capacity/headroom-sim) contains the sampling-based simulator (Python). Usage: 
  python simulate_headroom.py --cluster eu --samples 10000 --horizon 30 --rps-increment 0.25

- Admission controller APIs: documented in internal SDK (platformctl). Automations to invoke soft eviction are permitted only to SRE-runbooks service principal.

- Eviction impact simulator: integrates with cost-estimator tools to compute dollar delta and expected SLO benefit. Use for post-incident remediation planning.

Quality and safety guardrails

- Never perform hard eviction without approval from the Platform Manager and a logged communication to affected tenants.
- Any customer-visible mitigation must include an automatic rollback if regression in quality or unexpected errors occur.
- Maintain an immutable incident log that records every admission controller change; this log is required for sanity checks during postmortem.

Long-term initiatives and backlog suggestions

- Tenant hot-listing: proactively migrate high-risk tenants into dedicated pools when predicted annualized burn surpasses threshold X.
- Improve burst signalling in SDKs: provide tenants with a low-cost burst token API allowing planned bursts to be scheduled more cleanly.
- Integrate headroom predictions into deployment gates so new model variants cannot be routed to saturated pools.

Runbook appendices

A. Example CLI snippets
- Snapshot headroom probabilities: 
  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /etc/telemetry/token)" \
    "https://telemetry.redwood/api/headroom?cluster=gpu-cluster-eu&horizons=5,15,30,60" | jq '.'

B. Example incident evidence template (paste into postmortem):
- Incident summary: short text
- Timestamps: start, mitigations applied, recovery, escalations
- Headroom snapshots (attach JSON)
- Top-10 tenant table (tenant_id, tier, contribution tokens, burn%)
- Admission controller timeline (actions + actor)
- Suggested remediations and cost estimate

C. Example sampling configuration (YAML)
- samples: "10000"
- horizon_minutes: "30"
- granularity_seconds: "10"
- rps_increments: ["0.10","0.25","0.50"]

Related policies and references

- SLO governance guidelines: /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/slo-governance-manual
- Cluster admission controller API: internal docs in /confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/admission-controller
